title: Multi-step angle chase through a composite figure
subtitle: Lines, angles, and triangles · 15 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **15 of the official questions in Lines, angles, and triangles are this one** — 4 Easy, 3 Medium, 8 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The figure has several lines, often parallel lines plus a pair of crossing lines, two triangles sharing a vertex, or a polygon with one pair of parallel sides.
- The angle you want is not next to any given angle, so at least two facts have to be linked.
- These are often free-response questions at hard difficulty, sometimes with fractional answers.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Mark every given value on the figure and look for a triangle that contains the target angle or a vertical or supplementary partner of it.
- 2) Move known values into that triangle using vertical, linear-pair, or parallel-line relationships, one link at a time.
- For a polygon, extend a side to make a transversal.
- 3) Close with the 180 triangle sum or a straight-line sum, then convert back to the target angle if the target sits outside the triangle.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Not useful for the reasoning, which is spatial.
At most, use it to solve the final linear equation if the given values are expressions.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You stop at an intermediate angle, such as the triangle's interior angle, when the question asks for the exterior or supplementary angle next to it.
The wrong choices often include that intermediate value.
The other common error is assuming a right angle or a parallel pair that the question never states.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You stop at an intermediate angle, such as the triangle's interior angle, when the question asks for the exterior or supplementary angle next to it.
